RP1.name: Assigning 100% to an amount known to be only part of the original
RP1.example: £48 is 60% of the original, but label £48 as 100% and retain it as the whole. The original is 48 ÷ 0.6 = £80.

RP2.name: Using the percentage change instead of the percentage represented by the final amount
RP2.example: After a 20% reduction the price is £64; calculate 64 ÷ 0.2. £64 represents 80%, so divide by 0.8 to get £80. After an increase, use 100% plus the increase.

RP3.name: Multiplying by the forward multiplier instead of dividing
RP3.example: Undo a 20% reduction by calculating 64 × 0.8 = £51.20. Divide by 0.8 to recover £80.

RP4.name: Trying to undo a change with the opposite percentage of the changed amount
RP4.example: Undo a 20% reduction by adding 20% to £64, obtaining £76.80. The percentage is now based on a different whole; use 64 ÷ 0.8 = £80.

RP5.name: Converting the known percentage/multiplier with the wrong place value
RP5.example: After a 25% increase, correctly identify 125% but convert it to 0.125 rather than 1.25. For a final £100, divide by 1.25 to recover £80.

RP6.name: Failing to remove a separate fixed addition before reversing the percentage
RP6.example: A total of £69 includes £5 delivery added after a 20% reduction; use 69 ÷ 0.8 − 5 = £81.25. Remove delivery first: (69 − 5) ÷ 0.8 = £80.

RP7.name: Stopping at the recovered unit amount or scaling the wrong amount
RP7.example: One item costs £64 after a 20% reduction. Correctly recover £80 each but give £80 when asked for the original cost of three items. Complete 3 × 80 = £240.
